title: The fighter that took punishment

facts.text: The Hellcat began as an improved version of Grumman's F4F Wildcat and grew into an entirely new fighter, built to beat the Japanese Zero. The prototype first flew on 26 June 1942.
Production started in October 1942, before the prototype had finished testing. The Navy accepted the first production F6F-3 in January 1943.

It was built to take punishment: heavy cockpit armor, a bullet resistant windshield, self sealing fuel tanks and an armored oil tank, pulled along by a 2,000 horsepower Pratt and Whitney R-2800 engine.

On 10 November 1943, Ensign Byron M. Johnson of Fighting Squadron Two brought F6F-3 Number 30 aboard USS Enterprise, then on her way to the Gilberts. The fighter slammed into the carrier's port 20mm gun gallery and its ruptured belly tank caught fire.

The crash jammed the canopy and Johnson could not get out. Lieutenant Walter L. Chewning Jr., the catapult officer, ran over, climbed up the side of the burning plane, forced the canopy open and pulled him out.
Johnson escaped without significant injury. A Navy photographer caught Chewning in the act, and the picture became one of the best known photographs of the war.

Three and a half weeks later, on 4 December 1943, Enterprise and five other carriers of Task Force 50 sent 246 planes against Kwajalein and Wotje in the Marshall Islands. Their fighters shot down 19 Japanese fighters.
The Hellcat's best day came on 19 June 1944 over the Marianas, when Japan lost more than 270 aircraft to 26 Hellcats lost. It came to be called the Great Marianas Turkey Shoot.
Grumman built 12,275 Hellcats before production ended in November 1945. Hellcats were credited with a victory to loss ratio of 19 to 1.

photoNote: Tier: green. F6F-3 Number 30 of VF-2 nosed up in USS Enterprise's port 20mm gun gallery with its belly tank burning, 10 November 1943; Lt. Walter L. Chewning Jr. is climbing up the fuselage to pull Ens. Byron M. Johnson from the cockpit, gun crews in the foreground. U.S. Navy photo, National Archives 80-G-205473 (naId 520642), use Unrestricted. From the NARA TIFF (3000 x 2399), edges shaved, saved 1920 x 1530. Chosen for drama: a person risking his life inside the machine, and the whole Hellcat is in frame for the spec window (the plane and Chewning sit in the upper middle, good for the top half crop). Not taken on 4 December; the caption should give its own date. Runner up: Hellcats taxiing forward on Enterprise, 2 July 1943, 80-G-74510.
photoCredit: Lt. Walter Chewning climbs a burning F6F-3 Hellcat to rescue Ens. Byron Johnson, USS Enterprise, 10 November 1943. U.S. Navy photo, National Archives 80-G-205473, public domain.

F6F-3 Hellcats land on USS Enterprise after strikes on Truk, February 1944. U.S. Navy photo 80-G-59314, National Archives, public domain.

declassified.fact: Chewning was not a pilot. He was an engineer who had studied mechanical engineering at Cornell and worked at the Naval Aircraft Factory in Philadelphia before Enterprise. He received the Navy and Marine Corps Medal for the rescue, and after the war worked on aircraft research, including for NASA.

film.record: 428-NPC-1007, "Air attack on Marshall and Gilbert Islands: F6Fs crash land, burn on carrier" (NARA 75781)
film.license: U.S. Navy film, public domain (NARA use status Undetermined)
film.shot_notes: Same file as No. 116. 7 P.M. (this card): 01:16 to 02:10 an F6F Hellcat crash lands on a carrier deck, deck crew run toward it (01:20 to 01:36), the fighter bursts into flame (01:44, open here), smoke and a second landing (02:00 to 02:10); 05:28 to 06:00 TBF Avengers and an F6F in formation over the sea in color. No shot shared with the noon clip (00:14 to 00:36, 00:52 to 01:12, 02:36 to 02:52).
film.date_note: Late 1943 Gilberts and Marshalls carrier strikes, not dated to 4 Dec; the burning Hellcat is not identified. Caption it so.

video.note: 428-NPC-1007 (NARA 75781), faded color Navy film, silent. Cut 26 Nov 2026 (evening run) inside research's 7 p.m. stretches: 01:47.2 to 01:51.6 a Hellcat bursting into flame as it hits the deck, the fire running along the deck (opening on the fireball); 01:20.0 to 01:24.0 another Hellcat crash landing, deck crew running toward it; 05:38.1 to 05:41.6 Avengers and a Hellcat in formation over the sea; 05:51.5 to 05:54.5 an Avenger close among the clouds. Cropped to drop the burned in timecode along the bottom and the black film edges; 10:11 pixels scaled to square. Nothing from the noon clip (00:16.7 to 01:03.45).
